title: Work, Energy and Power
seo_title: Physics 1: Work, Energy and Power Worksheets (Strengthened SHS)
standard_text: Work done by a force; kinetic and potential energy; the work–energy theorem; conservation of energy; power and efficiency. (summary of the Strengthened Senior High School curriculum, Physics 1, Quarter 2)
meta_desc: Free Physics 1 worksheets (Strengthened SHS curriculum, Quarter 2): work done by a force, work and energy, conservation of energy, power and efficiency and power. 100 questions with answers.
body_html:
How to think about it

Work is done when a force moves an object: W = FΔx cos θ, where θ is the angle between the force and the displacement. A force perpendicular to the motion does no work. The work–energy theorem: the net work done on an object equals its change in kinetic energy.

Gravity is a conservative force (the work it does does not depend on the path); friction is non-conservative. Wnc = ΔEₖ + ΔEₚ. Power is the rate of doing work: P = W/Δt, and for constant velocity Pave = Fvave.

Example

A 50 N force pushes a box 4 m along the floor. Work?

W = FΔx

Answer: 200 J

Example

A 600 W motor runs for 10 s. Work done?

W = PΔt

Answer: 6 000 J

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the cos θ when the force is at an angle.
  • Thinking friction can be conservative.
  • Mixing up power and energy.

faq.q: Does the normal force do work on a car driving along a flat road?
faq.a: No, because it is perpendicular to the displacement.

faq.q: Why does a motor need more power to climb a hill quickly?
faq.a: More work must be done against gravity in a shorter time.
